parts.title: My grandfather's vegetable patch
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Every spring, my grandfather digs up a long strip of grass behind his house and turns it into a vegetable patch. When I was small, I thought he did it only because he liked being outside. Now I understand that growing food is his way of saving money and keeping busy since he retired.

Last April, I helped him for the first time. We planted potatoes, carrots and beans, and he showed me how to measure the space between the rows with a stick. 'If plants are too close,' he said, 'they fight for water.' I laughed, but he was serious.

The hardest part was waiting. After two weeks, nothing had come up, and I was ready to give up. My grandfather just smiled and told me to be patient. Then, one morning in May, tiny green leaves were pushing through the soil, and I felt incredibly proud.

By August, we were eating our own food every day. The carrots were small and a bit twisted, but they tasted sweeter than any I had bought in a shop. Now I plan to start a little patch in our own garden, and my grandfather has promised to lend me his best spade.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer's grandfather grow vegetables?
options: To sell them at a local market
To save money and stay busy
To win prizes at garden shows
To give food to his neighbours
questions.explanation: It is his way of saving money and keeping busy since he retired.

options: How to cook the vegetables he grew

questions.explanation: He showed him how to measure the space between the rows.

options: He was proud of his work
He was worried about the weather
He was cross with his grandfather
questions.explanation: Nothing had come up, and he was ready to give up.

options: The beans died in the cold
questions.explanation: Tiny green leaves were pushing through the soil.

parts.title: The garden behind the sports hall
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Two years ago, our school had an ugly corner of concrete behind the sports hall. [1] Then Mrs Kaplan, our science teacher, had an idea: why not turn it into a garden?

First, we had to break up the concrete, which was hard work. [2] Luckily, a local builder lent us a machine and showed us how to use it safely. After that, we filled big wooden boxes with soil and compost. [3] We planted lettuce, radishes and strawberries, because they grow quickly.

Not everything went well. In the first summer, the radishes were eaten by slugs, and a football landed on the lettuces. [4] Now we have a sign that asks players to be careful, and the slugs are kept away with a ring of crushed eggshells.

Today, the garden gives enough vegetables for the school kitchen every week. [5] Some of us have even started growing food at home, and the younger children visit the garden every Friday.
sentences: The best part is that the pupils eat what they have grown.
Everybody thought that nothing would ever grow there.
Her classes are always the most popular in the school.
Mrs Kaplan used to teach at a different school.
Every class was given its own box to look after.
Our teacher told us that the builder was her cousin.
Some pupils got blisters on their hands.

gaps.explanation: "Nothing would ever grow there" explains why the corner was ugly, before the new idea.
"Hard work" leads to blisters, and the machine arrives as a lucky solution.
Each class getting a box leads to "We planted" in the boxes.
The problems with slugs and the football are the mistakes that they learned from.
The pupils eating the vegetables is the best result of the garden giving food each week.

parts.title: A letter to Gran

Dad has built a small greenhouse [3] he can grow chilli peppers. Last week, it was so hot [4] I had to water everything twice a day. [5] I was away, my neighbour looked after the plants. I hope you can come and see them [6] you visit us in July.

questions.explanation: "So hot that" shows the result of the heat.

parts.title: Growing sunflowers
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Growing sunflowers is easy. Plant the seeds [1] a sunny place, about two centimetres deep. Water them every [2], and soon you will see small green leaves. When the plants are [3] tall as your knee, put a stick next to each [4] to keep it straight. Sunflowers need lots of water, [5] you must not forget them in hot weather. By August, your flowers will be [6] big as dinner plates.

gaps.explanation: "Every day" (or every morning) gives a regular time to water the seeds.
"As tall as" compares the plant with a knee.
"So" shows the result of needing a lot of water.
"As big as" compares the flowers with dinner plates.

parts.title: Starting a herb garden
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: hartley
turns.text: Hello, and welcome to Garden Tips. Today I’m going to explain how to start a little herb garden on your windowsill. First, you need a sunny window. Many people think any window will do, and a window facing north is fine for a cactus, but herbs need light, so choose one that faces south. East is the second best, but you will need to be patient. Second, the pots. You can use old cups, tins or plastic boxes, but there’s one important thing. They need holes in the bottom, otherwise the water stays in and the roots die. Put a plate under each pot. You’d be surprised how many people forget this. Next, the soil. Don’t take earth from the garden, because it is too heavy. Go to a shop and buy a bag of compost. It costs about five pounds, and it’s enough for ten pots. Fill each pot almost to the top. Now the seeds. Basil is my favourite for beginners. Press the seeds into the compost, about one centimetre deep. Some people push them deeper, up to three centimetres, but then they never come up. Then cover them lightly and water gently, with a small spoon if necessary. After that, patience! You have to wait three weeks before you pick the first leaves. The basil starts to appear in a week, but the leaves are too small to eat. Wait until they are as big as a coin. Finally, if you don’t want to grow from seeds, you can buy a small plant in a pot at the market for about two pounds. They are ready faster, but they die easily if you don’t give them enough light. And that’s all for today. Next week we’re going to talk about tomatoes. See you then.

gaps.explanation: North is fine for a cactus and east is only second best; herbs need a south window.

gaps.prompt: Make sure that the pots have ___ in the bottom
gaps.explanation: Without holes the water stays in and the roots die; the plate goes under the pot.

gaps.prompt: Instead of garden earth, buy a bag of ___
gaps.explanation: Garden earth is too heavy, so the speaker recommends compost from a shop.

gaps.prompt: Press the seeds in about one ___
gaps.explanation: Some people push them up to three centimetres, but then they never come up; one centimetre is right.

gaps.prompt: You can pick the first leaves after ___ weeks
gaps.explanation: The basil appears in a week, but the leaves are too small to eat; wait three weeks.

gaps.prompt: A small plant at the market costs about ___ pounds
gaps.explanation: The compost costs about five pounds, but a small plant is only two pounds.

parts.title: A garden designer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: dorothea
turns.text: Mina, you design gardens for a living. What first made you interested in them?

turns.speaker: mina
turns.text: People assume it was my degree, but I studied biology and honestly found it boring. I also worked in a plant nursery one summer, but I just carried boxes all day. The real beginning was my mother’s tiny garden, three metres by two. She grew everything in it, beans, roses, strawberries, and I spent every afternoon there as a child.

turns.speaker: dorothea
turns.text: When you meet a new client, what do you do first?

turns.speaker: mina
turns.text: Not the plan. That comes much later. I sit in the empty space for a few hours and watch where the sun falls, because that decides everything. Clients always want to talk about money first, but we do that on the second visit.

turns.speaker: dorothea
turns.text: What do you recommend to beginners?

turns.speaker: mina
turns.text: Don’t start with rare and expensive flowers, because they die and then you feel bad. Trees are lovely, but they need space and years. I always suggest plants that grow easily, like lavender or mint, that forgive your mistakes.

turns.speaker: dorothea
turns.text: What mistake do you see most often?

turns.speaker: mina
turns.text: Planting too many things. People go to a shop, see forty pretty plants, and buy them all, and a year later the plants fight for space. Cheap seeds are fine, they are often as good as expensive ones. And cutting back too much is rare. Most people don’t cut enough, actually.

turns.speaker: dorothea
turns.text: Which of your gardens is your favourite?

turns.speaker: mina
turns.text: A very strange one, on the roof of a car park in the city centre. We carried the soil up in buckets. It isn’t a hundred years old, it’s quite new, and it doesn’t belong to a school. It’s open to everybody. People have lunch there and forget they’re above the cars. That’s why I love it.

turns.speaker: dorothea
turns.text: What are you working on at the moment?

turns.speaker: mina
turns.text: I’m writing a book for children about gardening, with lots of pictures. People ask if I’m moving to Scotland, because I talk about it so much, but that’s only a dream. And I once thought about opening a shop in the city, but I’d miss the outdoors too much.

turns.speaker: dorothea
turns.text: Would you like to say anything to people who are afraid to start?

turns.speaker: mina
turns.text: Start with one pot on a windowsill. If it dies, try again. Every gardener has killed hundreds of plants.
